title: Charming e-cigarette users with distorted science: a survey examining social media platform use, nicotine-related misinformation and attitudes towards the tobacco industry
screen_reason: Cross-sectional online panel survey (N=1,225 young adults, June 2021) reporting, for each of six researcher-selected misleading claims about nicotine (three COVID-19-specific, three about nicotine in general), the share of respondents who RECALLED the claim (i.e. self-reported having encountered it in the last year): 12.53%, 10.35%, 10.78%, 14.02%, 31.09%, 20.79%. These are self-reported exposure shares with a survey denominator = RECALL (exposure). Belief shares reported alongside them are excluded by protocol (belief in false claims does not count), as are the summative index means.

estimates.platform: Online Qualtrics panel survey (channel of exposure not measured)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who recalled the claim that smokers are less likely to be hospitalised for COVID-19
estimates.denominator: 1,225 young adults aged 18-34 recruited through an online Qualtrics opt-in panel (convenience sample, oversampled for current e-cigarette users: 59.76%)
estimates.definition: Respondent indicated that they recalled the specific claim (i.e. reported having encountered it, in the last year); recall was assessed separately from belief
estimates.misinfo_def: Distorted science exemplified in this study by the extrapolation of published scientific findings to support unsubstantiated claims about a prospective therapeutic role of nicotine during the COVID-19 pandemic
estimates.source_quote: review cited above and was recalled by 12.53% with 11.65%
estimates.page_loc: Methods, 'Recall and belief of distorted science indices - COVID-19 related', p. 3
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Exposure is self-reported: the respondent said whether they recalled the claim, so ground_truth=self_report (as the schema requires for RECALL). The FALSITY of the claim, however, was set by the authors, not the respondent: The six claims were selected by the authors as 'distorted science' / 'misleading scientific claims' about nicotine, judged against the published evidence base (the authors state 'there is currently no evidence supporting a therapeutic use for nicotine with respect to COVID-19'); respondents only reported recall and belief, they did not judge veracity. No fact-checker or external list used; no reliability statistic for the indices.
estimates.moderator_quote: We contracted with Qualtrics to recruit N=1225 participants aged 18-34 years for a survey, fielded 4 June to 11 June 2021, to examine the relationship between exposure to and belief in distorted science about nicotine in general and in the context of COVID-19, social media use and tobacco industry attitudes.
estimates.notes: Verbatim percentage. One of six per-claim recall shares; the paper reports NO 'recalled at least one claim' share (only summative index means, M=0.33 of three COVID claims and M=0.66 of three general claims), so the six rows must not be summed. Exposure channel is deliberately unmeasured ('we do not assess whether exposure to such information occurred on social media in general or any specific platform'), so platform_norm=survey. Country is inferred, not stated. ground_truth is coded self_report because the exposure measure is the respondent's own recall; note that unlike a 'have you seen misinformation?' item, the six claims here were fixed by the authors, so what counts as misinformation is researcher-determined. source_quote is a single verbatim line of the .txt rendering: this two-column PDF interleaves the print columns line by line, so no full sentence is greppable; the moderator_quote, misinfo_def and rob quotes are reconstructed in the paper's reading order (contiguous within one print column, no ellipsis joins).

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) all six BELIEF shares (11.65%, 9.35%, 9.47%, 13.29%, 29.02%, 22.66%) - belief in false claims is excluded by protocol; (b) the summative recall/belief index means (recall M=0.33 (SD 0.74) of three COVID claims; M=0.66 (0.83) of three general claims) - scale means with no share of respondents above a threshold, so no row (they are also the only 'any of three claims' summary the paper gives, which is why no pooled recall share exists); (c) tobacco-industry belief shares (companies use candy flavours to lure young people 77.84%, spread false research about product safety 74.57%, politicians take money 80%, honest about safety 46.20%, part of the solution 39%, do good things for the community 48.90%) - attitudes/beliefs about the industry, not exposure to misinformation; (d) all odds ratios in Tables 2-3 (platform use predicting recall/belief; recall/belief predicting industry beliefs) - associations, not prevalence shares; (e) social-media platform use shares in Table 1 (e.g. YouTube 80.90%) - platform adoption, not misinformation. Judgement calls for the adjudicator: (i) the country is never stated in the text - United States is inferred from the authors' affiliation (Truth Initiative, Washington DC), the US race/ethnicity and high-school/GED categories, and the reference to the US Surgeon General; (ii) 'recall' is read as self-reported exposure to the claim, supported by the Results wording 'more likely to believe them, but not to recall exposure to them in the last year' and the Methods aim 'the relationship between exposure to and belief in distorted science'; (iii) the sample is a convenience opt-in panel that oversampled current e-cigarette users (59.76%) and screened out 495 attention-check failures whose recall was significantly higher, so these shares are not population estimates and the authors say so; (iv) breadth coded 'misleading' because the paper labels the items 'misleading scientific claims' / 'distorted science' (unsubstantiated extrapolations), even though some (e.g. propylene glycol sterilising the air) are closer to patently false. Quote note: the .txt rendering of this two-column article interleaves the left and right print columns line by line, so no multi-line sentence can be grepped. Every source_quote is therefore a single verbatim line fragment carrying the value; the moderator_quote, misinfo_def and rob quotes are reconstructed in the printed reading order (contiguous within a single print column, no ellipsis joins).

rob.design: Cross-sectional online opt-in panel survey (Qualtrics), fielded 4-11 June 2021, young adults aged 18-34; 2,088 consented, 495 failed an attention check, 90 removed for other quality-control reasons (e.g. straight-line responding), 278 removed for incomplete responses, final N=1,225; explicitly a convenience sample, not nationally representative, oversampled current e-cigarette users (59.76%); recall and belief measured with single self-report items for each of six researcher-selected claims, then summed into indices (no reliability statistic reported); ordinal logistic regression with robust SEs controlling for gender, race/ethnicity, education, current e-cigarette use and age; authors note recall and belief were significantly higher among respondents screened out by attention checks. Denominator sentence: 'We contracted with Qualtrics to recruit N=1225 participants aged 18-34 years for a survey, fielded 4 June to 11 June 2021'.
rob.item6_quote: Distorted science exemplified in this study by the extrapolation of published scientific findings to support unsubstantiated claims about a prospective therapeutic role of nicotine during the COVID-19 pandemic were recalled and believed more among more frequent users of Twitter and YouTube, but less among frequent users of Reddit.
rob.item10_quote: 'Nicotine by itself is no more harmful than caffeine from a cup of coffee' was recalled by 31.09% and believed by 29.02%.
